Revised assessment (anchored in the macro/finance literature):
- Key sentence: “The invasion and related events are creating additional upward pressure on inflation and are likely to weigh on economic activity.” A second policy‑salient line is the decision “to raise the target range for the federal funds rate to 3/4 to 1 percent” and begin balance‑sheet reduction on June 1.
- Literature context:
  • New Keynesian Phillips curve logic (expectations‑based) implies adverse supply shocks (energy, supply chains, pandemic) push inflation up and output down, worsening the policy trade‑off. A proactive, expectations‑anchoring stance aligns with inflation‑forecast targeting (Svensson and Woodford, 2005).  
  • Taylor‑rule style prescriptions and time‑inconsistency/average inflation bias arguments support front‑loaded tightening when inflation is far above target and labor markets are tight; this helps maintain credibility and anchor expectations.
  • Energy price shocks (oil VAR literature) and COVID‑related supply disruptions typically depress real activity while raising prices, consistent with the statement’s caution that Ukraine and China lockdowns will weigh on growth and add to inflation.
  • Credit/financial accelerator research (Bernanke–Gertler–Gilchrist) suggests rate hikes plus balance‑sheet runoff tighten financial conditions, which can dampen investment and future activity even if current business investment is strong.

Net takeaway: Tone is cautiously hawkish with downside growth risks and upside inflation risks. The forward guidance on ongoing hikes and QT, combined with supply‑shock uncertainty, leans negative for near‑term activity despite strong employment. Relative to a purely headline read, literature‑informed risk management nudges sentiment slightly more negative.
